title: Grade 9 Mathematics — Number Systems & Polynomials
description: Number Systems and Polynomials practice questions
subject: mathematics

questions.question: Which of the following is a rational number?
questions.explanation: √4 = 2, which can be expressed as 2/1 (a ratio of two integers). √2, √3, and √5 are irrational numbers.

questions.question: Every integer is a:
questions.explanation: Every integer n can be written as n/1, which satisfies the definition of a rational number (p/q, q ≠ 0). Not every integer is natural or whole (e.g., negative integers).

questions.question: The decimal expansion of a rational number is:
questions.explanation: Rational numbers have decimal expansions that either terminate (e.g., 0.25) or repeat in a pattern (e.g., 1/3 = 0.333...). Non-terminating non-repeating decimals are irrational.

questions.question: The value of (√5 + √3)(√5 − √3) is:
questions.explanation: Using the identity (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²: (√5)² − (√3)² = 5 − 3 = 2.

questions.question: The rationalising factor of 1/(√3 + √2) is:
questions.explanation: To rationalise 1/(√3 + √2), multiply by (√3 − √2)/(√3 − √2). The denominator becomes (√3)² − (√2)² = 3 − 2 = 1.

questions.question: The value of 2^(1/3) × 2^(1/6) is:
questions.explanation: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. So the answer is 2^(1/2) = √2.

questions.question: How many irrational numbers lie between √2 and √3?
questions.explanation: Between any two distinct real numbers, there are infinitely many real numbers — including infinitely many irrational numbers. Between √2 ≈ 1.414 and √3 ≈ 1.732 there are countless irrationals.

questions.question: Which of the following is the simplest form of (√45 − 3√20 + 4√5)?
A polynomial of degree 1 is called:
questions.explanation: A polynomial of degree 1 (highest power = 1) is a linear polynomial, e.g., 2x + 3.

questions.question: The zero of the polynomial p(x) = 2x + 6 is:
questions.explanation: Set p(x) = 0: 2x + 6 = 0 → x = −3. The zero is where the polynomial equals zero.

questions.question: Using the remainder theorem, the remainder when p(x) = x³ − 3x² + x + 1 is divided by (x − 1) is:
questions.explanation: By the remainder theorem, remainder = p(1) = 1 − 3 + 1 + 1 = 0. Since remainder = 0, (x − 1) is a factor of p(x).

questions.question: The factorisation of x² + 5x + 6 is:
questions.explanation: We need two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3. So x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3).

questions.question: Using the identity, the value of (101)² is:
If p(x) = x² − 4 and x = 2, then p(2) =
questions.explanation: p(2) = 2² − 4 = 4 − 4 = 0. Since p(2) = 0, x = 2 is a zero of the polynomial and (x − 2) is a factor.

questions.question: Factorise using factor theorem: x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 given that x = 1 is a root.
questions.explanation: Since x=1 is a root, (x−1) is a factor. Dividing: x³−6x²+11x−6 = (x−1)(x²−5x+6) = (x−1)(x−2)(x−3).
